content: Progestin-only pills (POPs) are immediately effective upon discontinuation, with no delay in the return of fertility. However, they do not provide protection against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). POPs are considered safe and suitable for nearly all women, including those who are breastfeeding (they can start immediately postpartum), women who have or have not had children, women who are married or unmarried, women of any age (including adolescents and women over 40), women who have recently had an abortion, miscarriage, or ectopic pregnancy, smokers (regardless of age or the number of cigarettes smoked), women with anemia (current or past), women with varicose veins, and women living with HIV (whether or not they are on antiretroviral therapy). When prescribing POPs, healthcare providers should give as many packs as possible, ideally up to a year’s supply (e.g., 11 packs of 35 pills or 13 packs of 28 pills). It is important to explain the pill pack to the patient, including whether it contains 28 or 35 pills. All pills in a POP pack are the same color and contain active hormones that prevent pregnancy. Patients should be shown how to take the first pill and how to follow the directions or arrows on the pack for subsequent pills. Key instructions for POP use include taking one pill daily until the pack is empty. Women who are not breastfeeding should take the pill at the same time each day, as taking it more than three hours late reduces its effectiveness. Linking pill-taking to a daily activity, such as brushing teeth, can help with adherence. When starting a new pack, the first pill should be taken the day after finishing the previous pack. Starting a new pack late increases the risk of pregnancy. Backup contraceptive methods may be needed in certain situations, such as when pills are missed or taken late. Backup methods include abstinence, male or female condoms, spermicides, and withdrawal, though spermicides and withdrawal are the least effective. If possible, provide condoms to the patient. If three or more pills are missed, emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs) can be considered. Patients should be informed that the effectiveness of POPs decreases when breastfeeding stops. Without the additional contraceptive effect of breastfeeding, POPs are less effective than most other hormonal methods. Women who stop breastfeeding can continue using POPs if satisfied with the method or may switch to another method. Common side effects of POPs include changes in bleeding patterns, such as prolonged postpartum amenorrhea in breastfeeding women, frequent or irregular bleeding, infrequent bleeding, prolonged bleeding, or no monthly bleeding. Other possible side effects include headaches, dizziness, mood changes, breast tenderness, abdominal pain, nausea, and, for non-breastfeeding women, enlarged ovarian follicles. Patients should be reassured that side effects are not signs of illness and that the absence of bleeding does not indicate pregnancy. Most side effects diminish or stop within the first few months of use, though bleeding changes may persist. If side effects are bothersome, patients should continue taking POPs to avoid the risk of pregnancy and can try taking pills with food or at bedtime to reduce nausea. They should be encouraged to return for help if side effects persist or if they have other concerns. In special cases, clinical judgment is required to determine whether a woman with certain conditions can use POPs. These conditions include acute blood clots in the deep veins of the legs or lungs, a history of breast cancer more than five years ago with no recurrence, severe cirrhosis or liver tumors, systemic lupus erythematosus with positive or unknown antiphospholipid antibodies, or the use of medications such as barbiturates, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, primidone, topiramate, rifampicin, or rifabutin, which reduce the effectiveness of POPs. In such cases, a backup contraceptive method should also be used. For continuing users of POPs, healthcare providers should regularly check on the patient’s satisfaction with the method, address any concerns (especially about bleeding changes), and provide strategies for remembering to take pills daily. Adolescents may require additional support. Providers should supply as many pill packs as possible, ideally up to a year’s supply, and plan the next resupply visit before the patient runs out of pills. Long-term users should be asked about any new health problems or major life changes, such as plans for having children or changes in STI/HIV risk, and follow up as needed. Combined oral contraceptives (COCs), also known as the pill, contain low doses of two hormones, a progestin and an estrogen, which are similar to the natural hormones progesterone and estrogen in a woman’s body. COCs primarily work by preventing ovulation. Their effectiveness depends on consistent use, with the greatest risk of pregnancy occurring when a woman starts a new pack three or more days late or misses three or more pills near the beginning or end of a pack. When used correctly, less than one pregnancy per 100 women occurs in the first year of use. Fertility returns immediately after stopping COCs, but they do not protect against STIs. COCs are safe and suitable for nearly all women, including those who have or have not had children, are married or unmarried, are of any age (including adolescents and women over 40), have given birth and are breastfeeding after a certain period, have recently had an abortion, miscarriage, or ectopic pregnancy, are under 35 and smoke, have anemia, have varicose veins, or are living with HIV (whether or not on antiretroviral therapy). When prescribing COCs, provide up to a year’s supply (e.g., 13 packs) based on the patient’s preference and planned use. Explain the pill pack, including whether it contains 21 or 28 pills. For 28-pill packs, the last seven pills are a different color and do not contain hormones. Show the patient how to take the first pill and follow the directions or arrows on the pack for subsequent pills. Key instructions for COC use include taking one pill daily until the pack is empty. Linking pill-taking to a daily activity, such as brushing teeth, can help with adherence. Taking pills at the same time each day helps with remembering and may reduce side effects. For 28-pill packs, the first pill from the next pack should be taken the day after finishing the previous pack. For 21-pill packs, the patient should wait seven days (no more) after finishing the last pill before starting the next pack. Starting a new pack late increases the risk of pregnancy. Backup contraceptive methods may be needed if pills are missed. Backup methods include abstinence, male or female condoms, spermicides, and withdrawal, though spermicides and withdrawal are the least effective. Provide condoms if possible. If three or more hormonal pills are missed, emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs) can be considered. Common side effects of COCs include changes in bleeding patterns (e.g., lighter, shorter, and more regular monthly bleeding, irregular bleeding, infrequent bleeding, or no monthly bleeding), headaches, dizziness, nausea, breast tenderness, weight changes, mood changes, and acne (which may improve or worsen but usually improves). Blood pressure may increase slightly but typically returns to normal after stopping COCs. Side effects are not signs of illness and usually diminish or stop within the first few months of use. Patients should continue taking COCs to avoid the risk of pregnancy and can take pills with food or at bedtime to reduce nausea. They should be encouraged to return for help if side effects persist or if they have other concerns. In special cases, clinical judgment is required to determine whether a woman with certain conditions can use COCs. These conditions include being less than three weeks postpartum and not breastfeeding, being between three and six weeks postpartum with additional risk factors for venous thromboembolism (VTE), primarily breastfeeding between six weeks and six months postpartum, being 35 or older and smoking fewer than 15 cigarettes per day, having high blood pressure (systolic 140–159 mmHg or diastolic 90–99 mmHg), having controlled high blood pressure with ongoing evaluation, having a history of high blood pressure where blood pressure cannot be measured, having a history of jaundice while using COCs, having gallbladder disease, being 35 or older with migraines without aura, being younger than 35 with migraines without aura that worsen with COC use, having a history of breast cancer more than five years ago with no recurrence, having diabetes for more than 20 years or with complications, having multiple risk factors for arterial cardiovascular disease, or taking medications that reduce the effectiveness of COCs (e.g., barbiturates, carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin). Backup contraceptive methods should be used in these cases. For continuing users of COCs, healthcare providers should regularly check on the patient’s satisfaction with the method, address any concerns (especially about bleeding changes), and provide strategies for remembering to take pills daily. Adolescents may require additional support. Providers should supply as many pill packs as possible, ideally up to a year’s supply, and plan the next resupply visit before the patient runs out of pills. Blood pressure should be checked annually if possible. Long-term users should be asked about any new health problems or major life changes, such as plans for having children or changes in STI/HIV risk, and follow up as needed.
